@how own mechanism: When a single argument cannot handle all situations, partition into cases and handle each one. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

! conclusion: 
  When a single argument cannot handle all situations, partition into cases and handle each one.

  + context: You are trying to prove a statement that behaves differently depending on some
    condition or parameter value.

  + IF:
      The objects or hypotheses fall into a finite number of qualitatively different types,
      and the proof technique that works for one type fails for another.

  + HOWEVER:
      Too many cases make a proof unreadable and suggest you are missing a unifying idea.
      If you find yourself with more than 3-4 cases, consider whether a different approach
      (symmetry, abstraction, contradiction) would eliminate the case split entirely.

  + THEN:
      Identify the exhaustive partition. Prove the result separately for each case. Verify
      the cases are exhaustive (no gaps) and handle any overlap. Common splits: positive/
      negative/zero, finite/infinite, convergent/divergent, trivial/non-trivial.

  + BECAUSE:
      Case analysis is often the simplest proof strategy available, even if not the most
      elegant. Many results in combinatorics, number theory, and real analysis require it
      because the underlying structure genuinely behaves differently in different regimes.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Identify the natural partition of your domain or hypothesis.]
    next[Verify the cases are exhaustive.]
    next[Prove each case, noting where the proof differs.]

@flexiarg math-informal-CA/estimate-by-bounding
@title Estimate by Bounding
@sigils [🔸/小]
@keywords bound, estimate, inequality, upper, lower, dominate, majorise, triangle, Cauchy-Schwarz, Jensen
@audience mathematicians, analysts, probabilists
@tone heuristic
@factor Endurance (khanti)

! conclusion: 
  Replace a complicated quantity with a simpler bound that is good enough.

  + context: You need to control a quantity (an integral, a sum, a probability, a norm) but
    exact computation is infeasible or unnecessary.

  + IF:
      You need an upper bound (or lower bound) rather than an exact value, and standard
      inequalities (triangle, Cauchy-Schwarz, Jensen, Markov, Chebyshev, AM-GM) are
      available.

  + HOWEVER:
      Bounds lose information. A bound that is too loose is useless. The art is in choosing
      the tightest bound that remains tractable. Chaining too many inequalities can
      accumulate slack to the point of triviality.

  + THEN:
      Identify which direction you need (upper or lower). Apply the most appropriate
      standard inequality. Check that the resulting bound is tight enough for your
      purposes. If not, try a different inequality or a more refined decomposition
      before bounding.

  + BECAUSE:
      Estimation is the engine of analysis and probability. Most theorems in these fields
      are proved by chains of inequalities, each replacing something complicated with
      something simpler. Knowing which inequality to reach for is a core skill.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Determine whether you need an upper or lower bound.]
    next[Identify candidate inequalities from your toolbox.]
    next[Apply and check tightness — is the bound strong enough?]

@flexiarg math-informal-CA/show-both-inequalities
@title Show Both Inequalities
@sigils [🔺/今]
@keywords equality, sandwich, squeeze, both-directions, inclusion, subset, superset, le, ge
@audience mathematicians, students, proof-writers
@tone heuristic
@factor Determination (adhiṭṭhāna)

! conclusion: 
  To prove equality, prove inequality in both directions.

  + context: You want to show A = B (where A, B are numbers, sets, or objects in an ordered structure)
    and no direct computation yields both sides at once.

  + IF:
      Direct computation of A or B is infeasible, but you can bound A from above by B and
      from below by B (or equivalently, show A is a subset of B and B is a subset of A).

  + HOWEVER:
      The two directions may require completely different techniques. One direction is often
      trivial while the other requires the bulk of the work. Identifying which is which
      saves effort.

  + THEN:
      Prove A <= B and B <= A separately (or A is a subset of B and B is a subset of A).
      Combine to conclude A = B. For the squeeze/sandwich variant: bound A from above and
      below by quantities that both converge to the same limit.

  + BECAUSE:
      This is one of the most common proof structures in analysis (sandwich theorem, integral
      bounds), set theory (Cantor-Bernstein), and algebra (showing ideals or subgroups are
      equal). It reduces equality to two often-simpler one-directional claims.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Determine which direction is easier.]
    next[Prove the easy direction first to build intuition.]
    next[Prove the hard direction.]

@flexiarg math-formalization-CA/uniform-continuity-boundedness
@title Bound the Image Before Controlling the Quotient
@keywords uniform-continuity, boundedness, image, quotient, denominator, api-chain
@audience lean-provers, formalizers, analysts
@tone procedural
@difficulty intermediate
@why math-informal-CA/estimate-by-bounding
@see-also math-formalization-CA/metric-cauchy-convergence math-strategy/proof-architecture
@how own mechanism: When an estimate involves a quotient of uniformly continuous functions, get the boundedness of the image first as its own lemma; the quotient control depends on it and cannot be obtained alongside it. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

! conclusion:
  When an estimate involves a quotient of uniformly continuous functions, get the
  boundedness of the image first as its own lemma; the quotient control depends
  on it and cannot be obtained alongside it.

  + context: An analysis obligation where a uniformly continuous function's
    values appear in a denominator or in a ratio, and the target estimate mixes
    the continuity modulus with the size of the values.

  + IF:
      The domain is bounded — or totally bounded — then uniform continuity gives
      a bounded image through a short chain of library steps, and that bound is
      the constant every subsequent quotient estimate needs.

  + HOWEVER:
      Attempting the quotient bound directly entangles two independent facts: how
      fast the function varies, and how large it gets. The modulus of continuity
      says nothing about the latter, so an argument that needs both and has
      proved neither separately will stall at a point where it is unclear which
      is missing. The order matters more than the difficulty: the boundedness
      step is short, and having it in hand makes the quotient step routine.

  + THEN:
      State and prove the boundedness of the image as its own lemma, via the
      uniform-continuity-to-bounded-image chain.

      Only then estimate the quotient, using that bound for the denominator and
      the modulus for the variation, keeping the two roles visibly distinct.

  + BECAUSE:
      Uniform continuity is a hypothesis about differences and boundedness is a
      conclusion about values, and the step between them is exactly where the
      domain's boundedness enters. Proving them in one motion hides that entry
      point, so a proof that fails gives no signal about whether the domain
      hypothesis was too weak or the estimate was arranged badly. Separated, the
      failure names itself.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Prove the image is bounded as a standalone lemma from uniform continuity.]
    next[Identify where the domain's boundedness enters and state it explicitly.]
    next[Estimate the quotient using the value bound for the denominator and the modulus for the variation.]

@flexiarg math-strategy/proof-architecture
@title Decide the Proof's Architecture Before Proving Any of It
@keywords architecture, layers, reduction, decomposition, bridge, convention, problem-faithful, proof-shape, api-location
@audience lean-provers, formalizers, analysts
@tone strategic
@difficulty advanced
@cross-list [CA FA]
@why math-informal/separate-into-independent-pieces
@how own mechanism: Before proving anything, name the layers the proof will have and the reduction between each pair — including the layer that reconciles the problem's own statement with the library's conventions. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

! conclusion:
  Before proving anything, name the layers the proof will have and the reduction
  between each pair — including the layer that reconciles the problem's own
  statement with the library's conventions.

  + context: A theorem that mixes several kinds of work — a decomposition, an
    estimate, a transport between two notions, a library API whose definitions
    differ from the problem's — and where it is tempting to start at the first
    line and see where it goes.

  + IF:
      The proof decomposes into layers each of which can be stated and closed
      independently — regularity inside a disk and singular behaviour on its
      boundary; a strictly monotone subsequence extracted before an almost-
      everywhere argument; a contraction reduced to an inequality the library
      already has — then naming the layers first turns one intractable proof
      into several tractable ones, and the reductions between them become the
      things to look up rather than to invent.

  + HOWEVER:
      The layer that gets skipped is the one nobody counts as mathematics: the
      bridge between the problem's statement and the library's. A problem
      phrased with strict bad sets `{x | ε < |fₙ x - g x|}` meets an API phrased
      with closed ones `{x | ε ≤ dist (fₙ x) (g x)}`, and the cheap move is to
      silently replace `>` by `≤` and carry on. That is not a reduction, it is a
      change of theorem. The same applies to tail conventions (`N₀ < n` versus
      `N₀ + 1 ≤ n`) and to threshold choices that look like bookkeeping. Skipping
      the bridge does not remove the work; it relocates it to a place where no
      gate will look at it.

      The opposite failure is building machinery before checking whether the
      general case needs it. Verify the degenerate or equality case first: it is
      cheap, and it sometimes closes the problem or shows the heavy route is the
      wrong one.

  + THEN:
      Write the layers down as named statements before proving any. For each
      adjacent pair, say which reduction connects them and whether it exists in
      the library or must be proved. Keep a problem-faithful statement of the
      goal alongside the library-shaped one and make the translation an explicit
      lemma with its own proof — including the threshold arithmetic
      (`δ = min ε b.toReal / 2` and the `b = ⊤` case) rather than eliding it.
      Check the degenerate case before building for the general one.

  + BECAUSE:
      A proof's difficulty is rarely uniform across its layers, and the layer
      that fails is seldom the one that looked hard. Naming the layers first
      makes the hard one visible while it is still cheap to change route, and
      makes the translation layer — the one that silently changes what is being
      proved — an object with a name, a statement and a proof instead of a step
      nobody wrote down.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[List the layers as named statements before proving any of them.]
    next[For each adjacent pair, name the reduction and say whether the library has it.]
    next[State the problem-faithful goal and the library-shaped goal separately; prove the bridge.]
    next[Do the threshold arithmetic explicitly, including the infinite/degenerate cases.]
    next[Check the degenerate or equality case before building general machinery.]

@how own mechanism: Prove something locally (on small pieces) and then assemble the local results into a global one. (source: this pattern's ! conclusion line; L8 rationale-backfill, zai-1, 2026-09-05)

! conclusion: 
  Prove something locally (on small pieces) and then assemble the local results into a global one.

  + context: You want to establish a property of a large or complicated object.

  + IF:
      The object admits a decomposition into simpler pieces (open cover, partition, filtration,
      localisation at primes), and the property you want can be checked on pieces.

  + HOWEVER:
      Not every property is local. You must verify that local data can be patched: the pieces
      must be compatible on overlaps, and the patching procedure must not introduce new problems.

  + THEN:
      Cover the object with pieces where the property is manageable. Prove it on each piece.
      Check compatibility on overlaps. Glue the local results into a global one, using
      partitions of unity, sheaf conditions, or patching lemmas as appropriate.

  + BECAUSE:
      Local-to-global is one of the deepest recurring themes in mathematics: sheaf theory,
      Mayer-Vietoris, local-global principles in number theory, partitions of unity in
      differential geometry. The power comes from reducing a hard global problem to many
      easy local ones.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Decompose the object into local pieces.]
    next[Verify the property on each piece.]
    next[Check compatibility and assemble the global result.]

@flexiarg math-informal-CA/optimise-a-free-parameter
@title Optimise a Free Parameter
@sigils [🔸/小]
@keywords optimise, parameter, choose, best, minimise, maximise, sup, inf, epsilon, delta, t
@audience mathematicians, analysts, probabilists
@tone heuristic
@factor Discernment (paññā)

! conclusion: 
  When a bound depends on a free parameter, choose the parameter value that gives the best result.

  + context: You have established a bound or inequality that contains a free parameter
    (epsilon, delta, t, lambda) and want the sharpest possible conclusion.

  + IF:
      The bound is valid for all (or a range of) parameter values, and different choices
      yield different strengths of conclusion.

  + HOWEVER:
      The optimisation may be analytically intractable. In that case, a sub-optimal but
      explicit choice (often guided by dimensional analysis or balancing terms) is better
      than an opaque optimal one.

  + THEN:
      Differentiate (or otherwise optimise) with respect to the free parameter. If the
      optimum has a clean closed form, use it. If not, choose a value that balances the
      dominant terms — this typically gives the right order of magnitude.

  + BECAUSE:
      This pattern is the workhorse of concentration inequalities, moment methods, and
      approximation theory. The Chernoff bound, Bernstein inequalities, and Laplace method
      all follow by introducing an exponential parameter and optimising.

  + NEXT-STEPS:
    next[Identify the free parameter and its valid range.]
    next[Optimise or balance terms.]
    next[Substitute back and simplify the resulting bound.]

/-
! # APM a93A01: Uniform continuity ⟺ difference quotient condition

Let f : (0,1) → ℝ. Prove equivalence of:
(a) f is uniformly continuous on (0,1).
(b) ∀ ε > 0, ∃ N > 0, ∀ x,y ∈ (0,1) with x ≠ y,
    |(f(x)-f(y))/(x-y)| > N ⟹ |f(x)-f(y)| < ε.
-/

import Mathlib.Analysis.Normed.Group.Basic
import Mathlib.Topology.MetricSpace.Cauchy
import Mathlib.Topology.MetricSpace.Bounded

open Set Metric Filter

noncomputable section

abbrev I01 : Set ℝ := Ioo (0 : ℝ) 1

/-- Condition (b). -/
def DiffQuotientCondition (f : ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε →
    ∃ N : ℝ, 0 < N ∧
      ∀ x ∈ I01, ∀ y ∈ I01, x ≠ y →
        N < |f x - f y| / |x - y| → |f x - f y| < ε

/-- Uniform continuity of f on (0,1). -/
def UnifContOn01 (f : ℝ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε →
    ∃ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ ∧
      ∀ x ∈ I01, ∀ y ∈ I01,
        |x - y| < δ → |f x - f y| < ε

/-- Bridge: UnifContOn01 ⟹ UniformContinuousOn. -/
lemma unifContOn01_imp (f : ℝ → ℝ) (hf : UnifContOn01 f) :
    UniformContinuousOn f I01 := by
  rw [Metric.uniformContinuousOn_iff]
  intro ε hε
  obtain ⟨δ, hδ_pos, hδ⟩ := hf ε hε
  refine ⟨δ, hδ_pos, ?_⟩
  intro x hx y hy hxy
  exact hδ x hx y hy (by simpa using hxy)

/-- UC on (0,1) implies f is bounded on (0,1).

    (0,1) is totally bounded ⟹ f's range on (0,1) is totally bounded
    (via restriction + TotallyBounded.image) ⟹ bounded. -/
lemma unifContOn01_bounded {f : ℝ → ℝ} (hf : UnifContOn01 f) :
    ∃ B : ℝ, 0 ≤ B ∧ ∀ x ∈ I01, |f x| ≤ B := by
  have h_uc : UniformContinuousOn f I01 := unifContOn01_imp f hf
  have h_uc_restrict : UniformContinuous (I01.restrict f) := h_uc.restrict
  -- (0,1) is totally bounded
  have h_tb_I01 : TotallyBounded (I01 : Set ℝ) := totallyBounded_Ioo 0 1
  -- Transfer to subtype: TotallyBounded (Set.univ : Set I01)
  have h_tb_univ : TotallyBounded (Set.univ : Set I01) := by
    have h_emb := isUniformEmbedding_subtype_val (p := fun x => x ∈ I01)
    have h_iff : TotallyBounded (Subtype.val '' (Set.univ : Set I01)) ↔
        TotallyBounded (Set.univ : Set I01) :=
      totallyBounded_image_iff h_emb.isUniformInducing
    -- h_iff : ∀ s, TotallyBounded (Subtype.val '' s) ↔ TotallyBounded s
    -- We need: TotallyBounded (Set.univ : Set I01)
    -- Subtype.val '' Set.univ = range Subtype.val = I01
    have h_img : Subtype.val '' (Set.univ : Set I01) = (I01 : Set ℝ) := by
      ext x
      constructor
      · rintro ⟨⟨x', hx'⟩, _, rfl⟩
        exact hx'
      · intro hx
        exact ⟨⟨x, hx⟩, Set.mem_univ _, rfl⟩
    rw [← h_img] at h_tb_I01
    exact h_iff.mp h_tb_I01
  -- Image of Set.univ under restrict f is totally bounded
  have h_tb_img : TotallyBounded ((I01.restrict f) '' Set.univ) :=
    h_tb_univ.image h_uc_restrict
  -- (I01.restrict f) '' Set.univ = f '' I01
  have h_eq : (I01.restrict f) '' Set.univ = f '' I01 := by
    ext y
    constructor
    · rintro ⟨x, _, rfl⟩
      exact ⟨x.1, x.2, rfl⟩
    · rintro ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩
      exact ⟨⟨x, hx⟩, Set.mem_univ _, rfl⟩
  rw [h_eq] at h_tb_img
  -- Totally bounded ⟹ bounded
  have h_bdd : Bornology.IsBounded (f '' I01) := h_tb_img.isBounded
  -- Extract bound using isBounded_iff_subset_closedBall
  obtain ⟨r, hr⟩ := (Metric.isBounded_iff_subset_closedBall 0).mp h_bdd
  refine ⟨max r 0, le_max_right r 0, ?_⟩
  intro x hx
  have h_in : f x ∈ f '' I01 := ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩
  have h_sub : f x ∈ Metric.closedBall (0 : ℝ) r := hr h_in
  simp only [Metric.mem_closedBall, Real.dist_eq, sub_zero] at h_sub
  exact le_trans h_sub (le_max_left r 0)

/-- **(b) ⟹ (a)**. -/
theorem diffQuot_implies_unifCont {f : ℝ → ℝ} (hf : DiffQuotientCondition f) :
    UnifContOn01 f := by
  intro ε hε
  obtain ⟨N, hN_pos, hN⟩ := hf ε hε
  refine ⟨ε / N, by positivity, ?_⟩
  intro x hx y hy hxy_lt
  by_contra hcontra
  push_neg at hcontra
  have hxy_ne : x ≠ y := by
    intro heq
    rw [heq] at hcontra
    simp [sub_self, abs_zero] at hcontra
    linarith
  have hxy_pos : 0 < |x - y| := abs_pos.mpr (sub_ne_zero.mpr hxy_ne)
  have hquot : N < |f x - f y| / |x - y| := by
    rw [lt_div_iff₀ hxy_pos]
    have key : N * (ε / N) = ε := mul_div_cancel₀ ε hN_pos.ne'
    nlinarith [hxy_lt, hcontra, hN_pos, key]
  exact absurd (hN x hx y hy hxy_ne hquot) (not_lt_of_ge hcontra)

/-- **(a) ⟹ (b)**. -/
theorem unifCont_implies_diffQuot {f : ℝ → ℝ} (hf : UnifContOn01 f) :
    DiffQuotientCondition f := by
  intro ε hε
  obtain ⟨B, hB_nonneg, hB_bound⟩ := unifContOn01_bounded hf
  obtain ⟨δ, hδ_pos, hδ⟩ := hf ε hε
  -- B' = max B 1 ensures B' > 0
  set B' := max B 1
  have hB'_pos : 0 < B' := lt_max_iff.mpr (Or.inr (by norm_num))
  have hB'_bound : ∀ x ∈ I01, |f x| ≤ B' := fun x hx =>
    (hB_bound x hx).trans (le_max_left B 1)
  -- N = B' + B' / δ... actually just use 2*B'/δ to bound |f x - f y| ≤ 2*B'
  -- |f x - f y| ≤ |f x| + |f y| ≤ 2 * B'
  set N := (2 * B') / δ
  have hN_pos : 0 < N := div_pos (mul_pos (by norm_num) hB'_pos) hδ_pos
  refine ⟨N, hN_pos, ?_⟩
  intro x hx y hy hxy_ne hquot
  have hxy_pos : 0 < |x - y| := abs_pos.mpr (sub_ne_zero.mpr hxy_ne)
  -- From quotient > N: |x - y| < |f x - f y| / N ≤ 2*B' / N = 2*B' / (2*B'/δ) = δ
  have hxy_lt_δ : |x - y| < δ := by
    have h1 : |x - y| < |f x - f y| / N := by
      have h2 := (lt_div_iff₀ hxy_pos).mp hquot
      -- h2 : N * |x - y| < |f x - f y|
      rwa [lt_div_iff₀ hN_pos, mul_comm]
    have h_fdiff : |f x - f y| ≤ 2 * B' := by
      have hx' : |f x| ≤ B' := hB'_bound x hx
      have hy' : |f y| ≤ B' := hB'_bound y hy
      calc |f x - f y| ≤ |f x| + |f y| := abs_sub _ _
        _ ≤ B' + B' := by gcongr
        _ = 2 * B' := by ring
    calc |x - y| < |f x - f y| / N := h1
      _ ≤ (2 * B') / N := by gcongr
      _ = δ := by
        rw [div_div_eq_mul_div]
        field_simp
  exact hδ x hx y hy hxy_lt_δ

/-- **Main theorem**. -/
theorem unifCont_iff_diffQuot (f : ℝ → ℝ) :
    UnifContOn01 f ↔ DiffQuotientCondition f :=
  ⟨fun hf => unifCont_implies_diffQuot hf,
   fun hf => diffQuot_implies_unifCont hf⟩

end
